newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Former Australian PM warns APEC not to lose nerve.
newsitem.headline: Former Australian PM warns APEC not to lose nerve.

text.p: Former Australian Prime Minister Paul Keating warned the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum on Thursday not to lose its nerve in promoting trade liberalisation in the region ahead of a key meeting next month.

APEC could fail by losing its nerve in maintaining progress towards the trade liberalisation goals set in Bogor, Indonesia, in 1994 or by adding new countries to the 18-member group, he told an international business conference in Jakarta.

"It can decide that the Bogor agenda is too difficult and that it should seek bread and circus-like diversions in other areas," Keating told the 27th World Congress of the International Association of Finanicial Executives Institutes.
"If APEC goes down this path it will quickly lose its sense of purpose," he said in a speech before leaving for a private meeting with Indonesian President Suharto.

"Unless the Individual Action Plans submitted in Manila are ambitious and reflect a genuine will on the part of the APEC governments to live up to their Bogor commitments, unless the Ministers and leaders address the most serious problems facing the region, APEC will begin to lose credibility," he said.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
In November 1994 they pledged in the Bogor Declaration to achieve the goal of "free and open trade and investment" by 2010 for developed economies and 2020 for developing nations.

APEC ministers and leaders will meet in Manila on November 22-25, including the fourth leaders' summit since the organisation was formed with a ministerial meeting in Australia in 1989 when Keating was treasurer (finance minister) in the then Labor government.

Keating, prime minister from December 1991 until he lost office in elections last March, attended the previous leaders' meetings in Blake Island in the United States in 1993, Bogor in 1994 and Osaka in Japan in 1995.
Keating said an ineffective Manila meeting would mean APEC would certainly lose any potential to influence the outcome of the World Trade Organisation meeting in Singapore in December.
"The optics of this, right in our own region, will demonstrate to the world any lack of resolve on our part," Keating said.

"Youth festivals, food fairs, business exchanges and cultural extravaganzas are fine in their place. But if you catch more than a whiff of them on the periphery of APEC's operations, you will know something is wrong," he said.
Keating also argued against "taking the easy way out" and expanding APECs membership.
"In my view, we will lose APEC if the membership expands now, or if it ever expands too much," he said.

"Its potential will be lost because the agenda will become too diffuse, the focus on the links between East Asia and North America will be lost. APEC will find it convenient to split into separate sub-groups," he said.

"With larger numbers, real exchanges about genuine problems will not be possible. The meetings will become pro-forma discussions with pre-ordained outcomes. Leaders will over time -- and quite a short time, at that -- lose the motivation for meeting."
"APEC will revert to being a Foreign Ministers' meeting and then it will lose its capacity for dramatic change," he said.
